title: Steve Biko
summary: Steve Biko led the Black Consciousness Movement, which told Black South Africans to reject inferiority and organise for themselves. He died in police custody at 30.
caveat: His own writings, a biography by a close friend, inquest records and the Truth and Reconciliation Commission document his life and death in detail. Several towns on this route have since been renamed.

stops.title: Born in Tarkastad
stops.narration: Bantu Stephen Biko was born here and raised in Ginsberg township, outside King William's Town, by his mother after his father's early death.

stops.title: Expelled from Lovedale
stops.narration: At Lovedale College, Biko was questioned by police after his brother's arrest and expelled. He later said it was the start of his hostility to authority.

stops.title: St Francis College
stops.narration: He finished school at this Catholic boarding school, where he read widely and debated liberalism and politics.

stops.title: Medical school in Durban
stops.narration: Biko studied medicine in the "non-European" section of the University of Natal and lived in the student residence at Wentworth, where his politics took shape.

stops.title: SASO launched
stops.narration: Biko led Black students out of the white-led student union to found the South African Students' Organisation, launched at a conference here.
sources: Steve Biko, I Write What I Like (1978)

stops.title: Banned to King William's Town
stops.narration: The government banned Biko and confined him to his home district. He kept working, setting up community projects including the Zanempilo clinic nearby.

stops.title: Arrested at a roadblock
stops.narration: Biko and Peter Jones were stopped at a police roadblock outside the town and taken into detention.
stops.confidence_note: The marker shows Makhanda; the roadblock was outside the town.
sources: Truth and Reconciliation Commission of South Africa Report (1998)

stops.title: Detained in Port Elizabeth
stops.narration: Held naked and shackled in security police offices, Biko suffered a severe head injury during interrogation.
sources: Truth and Reconciliation Commission of South Africa Report (1998)

stops.title: Dies in Pretoria
stops.narration: Police drove him more than 1,000 kilometres to Pretoria in the back of a vehicle, and he died in a prison cell. An inquest found no one responsible; in 1999 the Truth and Reconciliation Commission refused amnesty to the officers involved.
sources: Truth and Reconciliation Commission of South Africa Report (1998)
